description: I’m an electrical engineering student interested in power systems, electronics, and space exploration. I’m working solo on Lunar Horizon Explorer, a web app that compares sunlight and Earth visibility at example lunar sites. I wanted to explore how these conditions affect solar power and communication with Earth, and make those engineering concepts easier to understand.
summary: Lunar Horizon Explorer is a small web app that compares how sunlight and Earth visibility affect a lunar mission. Users can compare two coordinate examples, move through time, and see Sun and Earth elevations, estimated solar output, and communication visibility. NASA mode uses Sun and Earth positions downloaded directly from NASA/JPL Horizons for November 15 to December 15, 2026. A separate sandbox lets users try custom coordinates with a simplified model. The app also compares horizontal and Sun-tracking panels and estimates the ideal storage needed during the longest dark period. I focused on making the power and communication trade-offs easy to see. It is an educational prototype with clear limits, including an assumed horizon rather than measured lunar terrain.
details:
I made Lunar Horizon Explorer to help people understand two basic questions about a lunar landing site: will the mission have sunlight for solar electricity, and will it have a direct view of Earth? I am interested in electrical engineering, so I focused on the connection between site conditions and the power system.

The app compares two sites side by side. Users can move or animate the timeline, read Sun and Earth elevations, and see approximate times to the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise or Earthset. The comparison includes sunlight availability, Earth visibility, time when both are visible, the longest dark period, and estimated solar energy. Users can change panel area, efficiency, orientation and an assumed obstacle angle. A constant-load setting gives a basic storage estimate for the longest dark period. Results can be exported as CSV.

NASA mode uses observer ephemerides retrieved directly from NASA/JPL Horizons for four example coordinates. The bundled data cover November 15 through December 15, 2026 UTC, with 721 hourly samples per site and body. The app interpolates between samples and evaluates 720 intervals for the period comparison. Exact API queries and raw NASA responses are included with the source data. The preset names describe coordinate examples, not surveyed landing candidates.

A separate synthetic sandbox supports custom coordinates. It uses spherical geometry with adjustable Sun declination and illustrative Earth wobble. The app labels this mode clearly so its outputs are not confused with dated NASA data.

I used HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app, Python to retrieve and format the NASA data, and ReportLab to make the PDF demonstration. The website runs without installation or an API key. ChatGPT/Codex assisted with brainstorming, research, coding, calculations, debugging, writing and visual design. No AI model runs inside the app.

The main idea is to put the position view, power calculation and site comparison together so users can see how one setting changes the result. For example, sunlight near the horizon can produce little power on a horizontal panel, while a tracking panel can capture more of it.

This is an educational prototype, not a validated mission-planning system. The horizon is a user-set constant angle rather than a measured terrain profile. Earth visibility does not establish a working radio link. The calculations exclude eclipses, thermal effects, dust and system losses. The storage estimate assumes a full battery at sunset and 100% usable storage, without checking recharge feasibility. Event times are approximate to about one hour. Future work would add measured LOLA terrain, wider date coverage, battery recharge calculations and a radio link budget.

Source code, NASA data retrieval scripts, and raw data are available on GitHub:
https://github.com/Kite1219/lunar-horizon-explorer
